newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists and Communists map poll strategy.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists and Communists map poll strategy.

text.p: France's Socialist and Communist parties, uneasy allies when not outright enemies for nearly 80 years, meet on Tuesday to try to hammer out a plan to beat the ruling centre-right coalition in May 25-June 1 elections.

Clearly expecting the talks to be difficult, both Socialist Lionel Jospin and Communist Robert Hue insisted they would aim solely to define goals rather than reach an official pact to govern together in case of victory.

Jospin, whose party is forecast by most opinion polls to win about 220 seats compared with only 25 or so for the Communists in the 577-seat national assembly, levelled a warning to Hue even before they met.
"The Communist Party must ask itself questions about its historical future, about its identity and about its position," he told an election rally late on Monday.
"The Soviet Union has disappeared and the movement which began in 1917 ended the way we know in 1989. That means all those who were involved in that must ask themselves real questions," Jospin said.
His strong words were apparently aimed at countering warnings by centre-right politicians of a "Red menace" which a Socialist-Communist government might portend for France.
The French Communist Party was long one of the most staunchly pro-Soviet in Europe, run on strict Stalinist lines.
Hue said that if the Communists participated in a cabinet, "it would show that the left has remained to the left".
The two parties differ on key issues including European unity and a single European currency, both of which the Communists oppose.
The Rally for the Republic (RPR) Gaullist and the centre-right Union for French Democracy (UDF) were also scheduled to announce their own common platform on Tuesday.
There are few ideological differences between the two ruling parties but personal rivalries on the right are rampant.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe of the RPR is leader of the joint campaign to preserve the coalition's majority in parliament following President Jacques Chirac's decision to call a snap election.
But the prime minister and aides have realised his record unpopularity is working against the coalition and have coyly hinted in recent days he is not certain to keep the post.
Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre put a question mark over Juppe's future on Monday with an ambiguous statement about who would hold the job if the right won the election.

"Taking into account what we have heard during the campaign, we will need a new team, a new prime minister and it will be up to the President (Jacques Chirac) to choose that new prime minister," Debre told France-2 television.
In French, Debre's words could equally refer to Juppe being replaced or reappointed.
The latest two opinion polls show the centre-right coalition heading for a narrow majority in the elections but also suggest about one-third of voters could change their minds.
